critique.good: Roles, engineer names and phone numbers remain on one line. The wider week column gives the schedule hierarchy a clear presence.
critique.problems: The notes are cramped and create a tall table with substantial empty space in the contact columns. The first date range still breaks before its final day.
critique.cause: The 192px notes column forces frequent wrapping, while the 125px week column is still too narrow for the longest date range.

critique.good: Names, roles and phone numbers stay intact, and the wider notes column makes the table substantially easier to scan than r0A.
critique.problems: All three date ranges break awkwardly, leaving short final lines. A date range in the notes also breaks across lines.
critique.cause: The 95px week column leaves only 74px for text; the 222px notes column still produces some breaks within longer phrases.

critique.good: The notes have the most comfortable measure and form compact blocks. Roles and phone numbers remain intact, and the two-row week groups remain clear.
critique.problems: Every engineer name breaks across two lines, weakening the quick association between the person and phone number. Two week dates still break across lines.
critique.cause: The 112px engineer column leaves only 91px for text, while the 110px week column cannot accommodate the longer date ranges.

critique.good: All engineer names, role labels, and phone numbers stay on one line. The merged week cells clearly group each primary and secondary pair, and notes wrap without splitting words.
critique.problems: The notes are narrow and often occupy four lines, making rows tall and leaving large empty areas under the contact details. Two date ranges break across lines.
critique.cause: The 150px engineer column preserves full names, but leaves only 207px for notes. The 110px week column is too narrow for the longer date ranges on one line.

critique.good: The wider notes column improves reading rhythm and reduces several rows to three lines. Roles and phone numbers remain intact, and the week groups remain clear.
critique.problems: Two engineer names wrap, making the contact column less consistent. All three date ranges break, and the last note still needs four lines.
critique.cause: At 135px, the engineer column cannot accommodate the longest full names; the 95px week column also constrains dates. Those savings give notes 237px.

critique.good: The week labels and date ranges have a clean, consistent two-line structure. Roles and phone numbers remain intact.
critique.problems: Three engineer names wrap, while narrow notes frequently require four or five lines. The resulting tall rows create large blank areas and weaken the relationship between contacts and their notes.
critique.cause: The 140px week column uses space that could support notes or names. The 130px engineer and 197px notes columns are both too narrow for a balanced contact-and-notes layout.

critique.good: All engineer names and phone numbers stay on one line, making the contact pair easy to scan. The week and role shading establishes a clear hierarchy, and the notes remain readable.
critique.problems: Every date range breaks across two lines, and two notes need four lines. The extra height leaves substantial empty space in the contact columns.
critique.cause: The 95px week column cannot hold a full date range, while the 222px notes column forces the longer notes into four lines. The 150px engineer column preserves full names but leaves less space for notes.

critique.good: The 242px notes column gives the action text more breathing room; five of the six notes fit in three lines. Phone numbers and role labels remain intact, and the rows read clearly across.
critique.problems: Three engineer names wrap, making the contact column less consistent to scan. All three date ranges also break across lines.
critique.cause: The 130px engineer column provides 109px of text space, less than some full names need. The 95px week column is too narrow for complete date ranges.

critique.good: The wider week column keeps the Week 15 and Week 16 date ranges together. Role labels and phone numbers remain intact.
critique.problems: The Week 14 date still breaks awkwardly before its final day, two engineer names wrap, and several notes are more fragmented. The resulting tall rows spread the contact information farther apart.
critique.cause: The 120px week column is still too narrow for the longest date range. Its additional width comes largely from the notes column, leaving that column at 212px; the 135px engineer column also cannot hold every full name.

understanding.purpose: Show who is on call each week, how to reach them, and when escalation or coverage arrangements apply.
understanding.reading: Readers locate a week, distinguish primary from secondary coverage, then scan across for the engineer, phone number, and any action they need to take.
groups: Week and role establish the schedule hierarchy; each week label serves two role rows.
Engineer and phone form the contact pair for each role.
Escalation notes qualify the contact and coverage information for the same row.
keep_intact: Phone numbers, so they can be read and dialed quickly.
Individual name and date components; engineer names should remain on one line where space permits.
may_wrap: Escalation notes can wrap at word boundaries.
Week labels can break between the week number and date range, using the height of their two merged rows.
Engineer names can wrap between given and family names if more space is needed for notes.

bad.why: The wide week column takes space from escalation notes, producing narrow paragraphs and unusually tall rows while leaving large empty areas in the merged week cells.
Every engineer name wraps, making the people assigned to each role harder to scan, while the wide week column leaves substantial unused space.

final.rationale: r1B gives the escalation notes enough room to read in short paragraphs while keeping most engineer names on one line and every phone number intact. Its week labels wrap across three lines, but remain clear within the merged cells that group each primary and secondary pair. The resulting rows have a steady rhythm, with extra height where the longest note needs it.

general: Give space to columns in proportion to their reading task and content, rather than making columns equal.
Keep critical identifiers intact and make row groups easy to scan; allow prose to wrap at natural boundaries.
specific: Phone numbers need about 153 px here to stay on one line.
The merged week cells can accommodate wrapped dates, freeing useful width for engineer names and escalation notes.

final.tradeoffs: r2A and r3A keep all engineer names on one line, but narrow the notes and split the Apr 8–9 date across lines. r2B gives notes slightly more room but wraps an additional engineer name.
final.uncertain: A designer who prioritizes scanning complete names may prefer r2A or r3A. The ranges are conservative estimates around r1B, with other columns adjusted proportionally to fit; they have not been individually rendered, and small width changes may alter line breaks.

A.why: Week labels and phone numbers stay intact, but the narrow notes column creates long blocks and several engineer names wrap. The wide week column leaves substantial unused space.

B.why: All engineer names and phone numbers remain on one line, making the contact details easy to scan. Dates wrap awkwardly and notes are somewhat narrow, but the rows remain clear.

C.why: Nearly equal column widths give excessive space to short roles while squeezing notes into very narrow blocks. Every phone number breaks across lines, and rows become unusually tall.

D.why: The generous notes column reads well, but every phone number wraps and several names and date ranges break across lines. That weakens scanning for contact information.

E.why: Phone numbers stay intact and the notes have useful space. Two engineer names wrap and the date ranges split, but the rows and week groups remain clear.

F.why: Phone numbers remain intact and the notes are reasonably readable. Three engineer names wrap, and date ranges split across lines, making the contact columns less easy to scan than in B.

reviews.unsure: B's split date ranges are a noticeable compromise; E gives the notes slightly more room but wraps two engineer names.

A.why: Equal column widths leave the notes cramped and split every phone number; the resulting tall rows make the schedule harder to scan.

B.why: Names and phone numbers stay on one line, and notes have useful space. The narrow week column splits each date range across lines.

C.why: Week labels and phone numbers read clearly, but several names wrap and the narrower notes column makes rows taller.

D.why: Phone numbers stay intact and notes read comfortably. Two names and the week date ranges wrap, slightly weakening quick scanning.

E.why: Phone numbers stay intact and notes have ample space, though three names and the week date ranges wrap.

F.why: The generous notes column improves prose, but every phone number wraps and several names and date ranges split, making contact details harder to scan.

reviews.unsure: B splits the week date ranges, while D gives notes slightly more space; the preference depends on how much weight readers place on scanning names intact.
